Max Verstappen has given his support and backing to Dries van Langendonck, but who is the 15-year-old Belgian? Jul 21, 2026 9:08am UTC Ahead of the Belgian Grand Prix last weekend, news surfaced that Max Verstappen had taken his first steps into driver development by giving backing to Dries van Langendonck. But who is the 15-year-old that has caught the attention of a four-time World Champion? Who is Dries van Langendonck? Van Langendonck is currently a McLaren junior driver, having joined the team's driver development programme in 2024 at the age of just 13 after winning the 2023 World Junior Karting title. A move into single-seaters beckoned last season, where the Belgian teenager became the youngest winner of a British Formula 4 race by winning on his debut at Donington Park. The 15-year-old also won the Iberia-based Formula Winter Series at the end of the year before returning for a full season of British F4 in 2026, where he currently leads the standings after winning four races. Verstappen answered questions about backing Van Langendonck before the Belgian GP Why has Verstappen supported him? Verstappen is no stranger to taking an interest in motorsport outside the realms of F1, having set up his own GT and sim racing teams. But this decision marks the first time that the Verstappen Racing squad will actively support a young driver in the lower ranks of single-seater racing. Speaking ahead of the Belgian Grand Prix, Verstappen gave his reasons for wanting to support Van Langendonck in his quest to reach F1. "Dries has been a big talent for a long time already in karting and I think you can spot quite quickly when someone is a little bit more special than someone else," said Verstappen. "I think that has carried on with what he is doing in F4 and that's why I think it's very exciting to try and help him, guide him, of course hand-in-hand from McLaren's side as well, to make the right decisions for his future. "He wants to get to F1 and I'm just trying to make sure that will happen in the future. It's an exciting project to be part of." Van Langendonck was in attendance at the Belgian GP with McLaren What does Van Langendonck think about Verstappen's support? Van Langendonck was present during the Belgian Grand Prix weekend with McLaren, where he will remain as part of the team's development programme as well as receiving support and guidance from Verstappen. "Max Verstappen has always been an idol for me. Growing up in Belgium, there was a natural connection to him, but beyond that he's an incredible driver and someone I've always admired," said Van Langendonck. "Verstappen Racing provides another layer of support and backing alongside McLaren, which will be important for my career. "It gives me access to additional resources and opportunities to continue developing as a driver, including extra simulator time at Max’s simulator facility. "Having support from both McLaren and Verstappen Racing means I can focus on improving every aspect of my performance and becoming the best driver possible." Van Langendonck hopes to reach F1 with the support of McLaren and Verstappen Van Langendonck's ultimate goal? Like every driver in the junior ranks, Van Langendonck hopes to reach F1 and believes that the support of McLaren and Verstappen together will allow him to get the most out of his potential. "Ultimately, my goal is to race in Formula 1 and obviously become a Formula 1 World Champion," he explained. "There's still a long way to go and a lot of hard work ahead, but I believe that's possible with McLaren and their support. "If I continue to develop, work hard and make the most of every opportunity, hopefully all the pieces will come together." https://www.armstrongeconomics.com/world.text: The Ukraine Money Pit — Estonia’s €70 Million Scandal Estonia’s Defence Minister Hanno Pevkur has resigned after a €70 million ammunition deal intended to supply Ukraine blew up into a procurement scandal. Estonia agreed to purchase artillery shells from Datasel, an Italian-registered company owned by India’s Neco Defense Munitions, despite the companies having no established history of selling artillery shells . Millions were paid in advance, deliveries ran into problems, Estonia terminated the contracts, and the dispute has now gone to arbitration. This is what happens when government declares everything an emergency and suddenly the normal rules surrounding public money become inconvenient. Pevkur says he did not negotiate the contracts and had not even read them. His explanation was rather revealing: “The defence minister does not conduct contract negotiations. The defence minister does not count socks and ammunition.” He said his responsibility was making the fundamental political decision to support Ukraine. He nevertheless resigned because the National Audit Office’s findings raised the question of political responsibility. At least somebody in government still remembers what that phrase means. The scandal goes directly to the problem with Europe’s entire approach to Ukraine. The politicians declare that Ukraine must be supported at any cost, and once you use those words, cost ceases to matter. Due diligence becomes something bureaucrats complain takes too long. Money must be spent immediately because politicians tell everyone that Europe itself will fall if another artillery shell does not reach Ukraine yesterday. Estonian officials have essentially admitted that extraordinary risks were accepted because of the urgency surrounding Ukraine. One official told reporters that they knew these procurements involved “greater risks than usual” but believed those risks were justified by what was at stake. There is the entire problem in one sentence. When government decides that the political objective is important enough to justify greater financial risk, taxpayers become the insurance policy when something goes wrong. Estonia’s National Audit Office had already raised serious concerns about defense spending and the activities of the Estonian Centre for Defence Investments. The issue is no longer merely whether ammunition arrived. There is now a possibility that Estonia itself could become responsible for tens of millions of euros tied up in the dispute, depending on how the contracts and EU financing are ultimately resolved. The European Commission says it is discussing whether Estonia may have to return the European funds and insists that safeguards exist to protect taxpayers. That is always what government says after the money has already left the building. The supplier disputes Estonia’s version of events and says it supplied and invoiced €58 million worth of material against €59 million in advance payments. Datasel also rejects allegations that the ammunition failed inspections and argues that regulatory approvals and documentation delays complicated the international supply chain. That dispute will now have to be resolved through arbitration, but it does not change the larger political question of how a procurement carrying this degree of risk was approved in the first place. Europe has thrown enormous sums into Ukraine under the premise that there is simply no alternative. The European Peace Facility was created before the invasion as an instrument supposedly designed to “preserve peace,” yet it has become a major mechanism for financing weapons. You have to appreciate government terminology. They create something called a Peace Facility and then use it to purchase artillery ammunition for a war. The Ukraine conflict has become another demonstration of how governments operate once fear eliminates fiscal restraint. Nobody is permitted to question the amount because asking where the money went is immediately portrayed as helping Putin. Nobody asks what the endgame is because that supposedly undermines Ukraine. Nobody wants to calculate what European taxpayers have actually committed because the answer becomes politically uncomfortable. This is precisely how accountability disappears. Europe has spent years telling its citizens that there is not enough money for pensions, healthcare, infrastructure, farmers, or tax relief. Governments insist they must raise retirement ages because the money is running out. They impose austerity when sovereign debt becomes unsustainable and then lecture ordinary people about living within their means. Yet when politicians want war, suddenly hundreds of billions can materialize. The money is always there when government wants it. Estonia is particularly interesting because it has been among the most aggressive European supporters of Ukraine relative to the size of its economy. Defense spending has surged since 2022 as the Baltic governments repeatedly warn that Russia could eventually attack NATO territory. That fear has become the political justification for enormous military expenditures throughout Eastern Europe, and now Brussels wants the rest of Europe to follow. This is how the military-industrial complex expands. You create permanent geopolitical fear, governments announce massive defense budgets, procurement must be accelerated, and taxpayers are told that questioning any expenditure threatens national security. The faster government spends money, the easier it becomes for mistakes, incompetence, favoritism, and outright corruption to hide inside the urgency. Europe is now preparing to spend vastly more on defense. NATO members have committed themselves to dramatically higher military expenditures while Brussels discusses expanding common defense financing and additional support for Ukraine. If governments cannot properly oversee tens of millions, what happens when the spending reaches hundreds of billions? The taxpayer always gets the bill. What makes this even more absurd is that European leaders insist all of this spending is necessary because Russia represents an existential threat, while simultaneously pursuing policies that have damaged Europe’s own economy. They sanctioned cheap Russian energy, drove manufacturing costs higher, increased military expenditures, expanded government debt, and then acted surprised when Europe’s economic competitiveness deteriorated. There is no strategic planning. There is only political reaction. The Estonian scandal should therefore be treated as a warning about what happens when war becomes an open-ended government program. The political objective of supporting Ukraine became more important than the financial risk surrounding the procurement, and now officials are fighting over who may ultimately absorb the losses while the defense minister has resigned. The €70 million dispute in Estonia may seem small compared with the hundreds of billions already committed to Ukraine and European rearmament, but that is precisely why it matters. War has always been the greatest excuse for government spending because fear silences questions that taxpayers would normally ask. Estonia has now discovered why those questions should have been asked before the money was transferred rather than after. https://www.thetimes-tribune.com/2026/09.text: The former St. Michael’s Church and rectory in the 1700 block of Jackson Street in West Scranton pictured Monday, Sept. 14, 2026. The Agency for Community Empowerment purchased the church and rectory and plans to convert them into an affordable housing unit and childcare center respectively. (Christine Lee/Staff Photo) By Christine Lee | clee@scrantontimes.com | The Times-Tribune PUBLISHED: September 14, 2026 at 4:53 PM EDT | UPDATED: September 14, 2026 at 5:05 PM EDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... Two buildings that served West Scranton’s spiritual needs will be repurposed to serve the need for childcare and housing in the neighborhood. The Agency for Community EmPOWERment, or ACE, purchased the former St. Michael’s Roman Catholic Church and its neighboring rectory building in the 1700 block of Jackson Street last month, according to a property transfer recorded by the Lackawanna County recorder of deeds. The Scranton-based agency plans to turn the rectory into a four-bedroom affordable housing unit, and the church into an early childhood center. Executive Director Jim Wansacz said the buildings fill a need for housing and childcare in the area. “We’re looking at this as a way to put in a family in (a home) at an affordable way, and also fill a need for more early learning classrooms,” he said. A community needs assessment conducted by the agency found a need for both in the neighborhood. ACE plans to convert the church into an early childhood center with two or three classrooms, serving infants and children up to 5 years of age. The number of teachers will depend on the type of classroom and guidelines for running them. Families will not be charged to enroll children at the facility. The agency has more than 1,000 children enrolled in early childhood facilities in Lackawanna, Wayne, Pike and Susquehanna counties. Wansacz said they help children get ready for school. The house will be part of the agency’s Scranton Lackawanna Resources Development Corporation, which matches low- to moderate-income families with affordable housing. ACE has 12 units throughout the county that it rents to families that meet the income qualifications, Wansacz said. “The housing will be taken care of for families that will be able to live in an affordable, high-quality housing,” he said. Wansacz anticipates the house will be ready for tenants by November or December, and the classrooms will be up and running next year. The former St. Michael’s Church on Jackson Street in West Scranton pictured Monday, Sept. 14, 2026. (Christine Lee/Staff Photo) The rectory of the former St. Michael’s Church on Jackson Street in West Scranton pictured Monday, Sept. 14, 2026. (Christine Lee/Staff Photo) Show Caption 1 of 2 The former St. Michael’s Church on Jackson Street in West Scranton pictured Monday, Sept. 14, 2026. (Christine Lee/Staff Photo) Expand The Diocese of Scranton closed the church last year, with its final Mass taking place last September. In his decree ordering the closure, the Most Rev. Joseph Bambera, bishop of the diocese, said the parish — which is overseen by the Priestly Fraternity of St. Peter and celebrates the traditional Latin Mass — had outgrown the church on Jackson Street and ordered the parish relocated to St. Lucy’s Church on Scranton Street. The church, originally established for Catholics of Lithuanian heritage, was dedicated in 1942, according to archives of The Times-Tribune. Felicia Gerrity, manager of Vitali’s Market, which sits next to the rectory, grew up attending the church and was married there, and two of her four children were baptized there. She was sad to see it close but is hopeful its new owner can bring new life to the building. “I think it will bring more people to the neighborhood, and it’s better than being empty,” she said. The buildings are the latest project for the nonprofit agency, which is part of a national network of federally funded community action agencies that administers poverty-assistance programs on the local level. Those include housing, early learning, home weatherization, utility, vehicle and food assistance, and workforce and veterans programs. They received funding last year for a new housing complex for veterans in South Scranton. The building at 601 Prospect Ave. will house up to eight veterans. It is also not the first former faith-based property the organization has acquired, as it uses the former Holy Rosary School in North Scranton as an early learning center. Last summer, the city awarded a $125,000 grant via federal funds to convert a vacant, run-down house in North Scranton into two three-bedroom affordable-housing units for two families. The agency is currently rehabilitating the building in North Scranton, which Wansacz said is of particular need in the community. “The number one need in community needs assessments is affordable housing,” he said. “Not only in Lackawanna County, but in the country. That’s why you hear people talking about that.” Wansacz sees the buildings’ future uses as good for the community. “We looked at this as a good deal that could provide a community service to the area,” he said.
